title: Mental distress and healthcare utilisation among sami and non-sami adults: a prospective registry-linked cohort study utilising data from the SAMINOR 2 questionnaire survey and the Norwegian control and payment of health reimbursements database (2012-2022)

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Mental distress and healthcare utilisation among sami and non-sami adults: a prospective registry-linked cohort study utilising data from the SAMINOR 2 questionnaire survey and the Norwegian control and payment of health reimbursements database (2012-2022)》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Aim · s0002-s2001-p1】The aim of this study was to investigate whether level of mental distress was associated with utilisation of primary and specialised healthcare services among Sami and non-Sami populations, and whether the impact of mental distress on healthcare utilisation differs between Sami and non-Sami.

【Introduction · s0002-p1】According to the World Health Organisation [1], mental health conditions such as anxiety and depression are common across countries and communities. They are a leading contributor to disability and impose substantial costs on individuals, healthcare systems, and society. Mental distress is also profoundly linked to physical health in a bidirectional pathway. Depression and anxiety frequently coexist with chronic conditions such as cardiometabolic disease [2], diabetes [3], and chronic pain [4]. As a result, individuals experiencing mental distress often have more complex healthcare needs, making mental distress an important determinant of healthcare utilisation across both primary and specialist care settings.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Mental distress and healthcare utilisation among sami and non-sami adults: a prospective registry-linked cohort study utilising data from the SAMINOR 2 questionnaire survey and the Norwegian control and payment of health reimbursements database (2012-2022)》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Materials and methods · s0003-p1】For the current study, data from the SAMINOR 2 Questionnaire Survey was linked to data on healthcare utilisation retrieved from the Norwegian Control and Payment of Health Reimbursements database (KUHR-database) and demographic information from Statistics Norway (SSB) for the study period 2012–2022. Linkage was enabled through unique Norwegian personal identification numbers, which was replaced by project-specific identifiers by SSB to ensure participant confidentiality.

【Introduction · s0002-p5】Still, barriers for use of health care among Sami mirror those reported for other Indigenous groups. The historical trauma leading to lack of trust in authority figures [13], and to communication challenges arising from linguistic and cultural differences between Sami patients and non-Sami health personnel [20], are likely to contribute to Sami refraining from use of health care services [21,22]. Strong cultural norms regarding privacy rendering open discussions of mental health inappropriate or stigmatised [23], may also impact on healthcare utilisation. While these cultural and structural factors are not measured in the present study, they provide an essential framework for interpreting potential differences in healthcare-seeking behaviour.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Mental distress and healthcare utilisation among sami and non-sami adults: a prospective registry-linked cohort study utilising data from the SAMINOR 2 questionnaire survey and the Norwegian control and payment of health reimbursements database (2012-2022)》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Results · s0004-p1】The study followed a baseline sample of 10,517 individuals from 2012-2022. Attrition due to emigrations and deaths was evenly distributed across sex and ethnic groups over the study period. Descriptive statistics for the variables included in the models are presented in Table 1. In both sexes, more Sami participants reported symptoms of mental distress above the cut-off score compared with non-Sami participants. Across all groups, high mental distress was consistently associated with lower education and the presence of chronic conditions. Sami individuals in both the high mental distress and low mental distress group reported having a chronic condition more frequently than non-Sami in the corresponding groups.

【Conclusion · s0007-p1】This study demonstrates that mental distress is associated with increased utilisation of both primary and specialist healthcare services among Sami and non-Sami populations, with only modest ethnic differences. While these findings suggest broadly comparable access to healthcare services, utilisation rates alone cannot fully capture differences in healthcare-seeking behaviour, care pathways, or experiences of care. Also, common living conditions, universal healthcare coverage, and longstanding cultural exchange between Sami and non-Sami populations may have contributed to converging patterns of healthcare utilisation in northern Norway. This may partly explain why the ethnic differences observed in the present study were smaller than those reported among Indigenous populations in other national contexts. Future studies should therefore move beyond measures of service use to examine how cultural, structural, and contextual factors shape engagement with healthcare among Sami and non-Sami populations.
